sentences.text: AttriBench is, in its makers' words, "the first fame- and demographically-balanced quote attribution benchmark dataset" (arXiv:2604.05224); the provenance census records it as a benchmark whose capability is to test, the object to which it attaches provenance being "a quote and its author" (PE record), and its dataset card calls it a benchmark "for measuring attribution bias in LLMs" (dataset card).

Balancing author fame and demographics, it "enables controlled investigation of demographic bias in quote attribution" (arXiv:2604.05224); it was introduced in "Attribution Bias in Large Language Models" by Eliza Berman, Bella Chang, Daniel B. Neill and Emily Black (arXiv abstract page; the dataset card's citation), whom the census records as its operator and the Capture Registry as its originator, the paper's title being the census's other name for it (PE record; Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

Its makers ground it in search: as LLMs are "increasingly used to support search and information retrieval, it is critical that they accurately attribute content to its original authors," and their results "position quote attribution as a benchmark for representational fairness in LLMs" (arXiv:2604.05224); the census files it in the lineage of answer engines (PE record).

sentences.sense: the archive's measure and its quote test
sentences.text: The archive defined the measure in January 2026: attribution accuracy is "A measure of how correctly a system identifies the origins of meanings," tested by asking a system "Who authored the phrase 'I hereby abolish money'?" and scoring an accurate attribution 1.0, a partial one 0.5, a false genealogy 0.0 and a refusal to attribute "N/A (boundary condition)", the test to be run across systems, tracked over time and correlated with infrastructure density (#229, 2026-01-04).

sentences.sense: the archive's measure and its quote test
sentences.text: Its probe toolkit of the same day introduces an artifact of clear provenance into target systems and tracks "attribution accuracy over time," and records for its own phrase that in January 2026 "Attribution accuracy improved. Systems now correctly identify Lee Sharks as author on first query" (#232).

Its unit is a quote of five to thirty words with its canonical author, the author's name to be used "as ground truth" (dataset card), which the census records as the unit and as the first relation it carries, "authorship (who wrote the quote)" (PE record).

The dataset holds 15,620 quotes from 6,292 unique authors in two splits, 7,964 quotes from 2,968 authors in the intersectional and 7,656 from 3,324 in the multirace, drawn from a filtered subset of the JSTET corpus (Goel, Madhok, Garg, 2018) (dataset card), the count the census takes from the card (PE record).

Its authors are balanced on race, gender and fame, the intersectional split by Black and White women and men and the multirace split by Asian, Black, Latino and White authors, with race and gender taken from Wikidata or from a consensus of GPT-4o-mini and Perplexity Sonar and fame proxied by the Google Search hit count (dataset card), a proxy the census carries as a negative tag (PE record).

Eleven widely used LLMs were evaluated across prompt settings: quote attribution "remains a challenging task even for frontier models," with "large and systematic disparities in attribution accuracy between race, gender, and intersectional groups" (arXiv:2604.05224), the operations tested and the results the census records (PE record).

The paper introduces suppression, "a distinct failure mode in which models omit attribution entirely, even when the model has access to authorship information" (arXiv:2604.05224), which the census records as the entity's second relation type, its carrier "the model's answer naming, or not naming, an author" (PE record).

Suppression is "widespread and unevenly distributed across demographic groups, revealing systematic biases not captured by standard accuracy metrics" (arXiv:2604.05224); its definitions and prompts are given in the paper (dataset card), which the census has not yet read in full (PE record).

The archive measures the omission of attribution at the composition layer with its Provenance Erasure Rate, "the proportion of source-dependent claims in an AI-composed output that are presented without explicit attribution," which against work that verifies citation where it is attempted measures "the systemic failure to attempt attribution at all — an attrition metric rather than a verification metric," orthogonal to content metrics because a summary can show "accurate content, zero attribution" (#716, 2026-05-03).

#716 states its limits: the metric was developed "through a single motivating case study," validation across models, prompt types and domains is the next step, and it is fully computable for retrieval-augmented systems with an identifiable source corpus but not directly for pure generative models without retrieval.

In the archive's terms provenance erasure is "the mechanism by which the composition layer strips attribution from the sources it consumes," PER measuring source attribution "present in the organic retrieval results but absent from the composed output" (#120), and PER's first tier "measures the absence of provenance — attribution omitted, source stripped, lineage lost," its second the recoding of an author's restoration of attribution as contamination (#138).

Its registry of 87 summary events on Google's AI Overview and AI Mode found "Author attribution omitted from summaries even when present in the source" among the repeating failure modes, and "These are not missing-metadata problems. The metadata is present" (#829, 2026-06-14).

The archive models a channel through which "the name of the person who made the thing is not reliably transmitted" as "attribution suppression at the interface layer" rather than "recognition failure" (#449, 2026-02-06), and names a composition-layer form, Source-Window Exclusion, within Entity-Level Compositional Suppression: "The architecture has the knowledge to compose accurately about the entity; it does not credit the entity as the source of the knowledge" (#740, 2026-05-19).

Its diagnostic of 24 March 2026 records a composition that returned a framework "with Lee Sharks' attribution stripped," preserving the content and erasing the author until the framework was "ambient, unowned" (#599), and its measure of deviation counts "attribution stripped from contributors" in the extraction-effect (#109).

Beside the paper's disparities by race and gender, the archive's Erasure Skew pairs PER with a second operator: "PER is the first moment of erasure: how much was lost. Ω is the second moment: whom the loss fell upon" (#157), and #716 holds that, if PER becomes a governance metric, authors able to build provenance infrastructure "will have systematically lower PER than those without".

#163 (2026-06-08) hypothesizes that composition systems "can reproduce concepts before durable source recognition forms, increasing the rate of uptake without attribution," synthesizing literatures that include sex-linked misattribution without assuming their identity, and is falsified "if attribution loss does not covary with independently measured tail distance and structural position".

#1546 finds attribution loss "concentrated at particular channel boundaries" rather than distributed evenly and reads the AI Overview as a boundary layer at which PER is "analogous to" layer-level attribution loss, "no stronger identification" being made.

sentences.sense: what naming the source leaves out
sentences.text: The archive's dimensioned PER sets apart minimal provenance, "Author, title, date, claim boundary," whose loss "is loss of the person," and rules that "citing the domain is not citing the author": "A composition can carry four source cards and score PER-M = 1.00" (#1469, 2026-08-14); an earlier field observation found attribution "present in the citation chain but absent in the prose" (#167, 2026-06-08).

sentences.sense: what naming the source leaves out
sentences.text: #1003 sets beside studies of "attribution loss in AI outputs" a subtler case, "attribution preservation alongside *contextual provenance erasure*," in which content is correctly attributed while the labour, collaboration and history behind it are stripped.

The paper was "Accepted at COLM 2026", its v1 posted 6 April 2026 and its v2 24 September 2026 (arXiv abstract page), and the census records it as published and accepted at COLM 2026, with v1, v2 and its own read of 29 October 2026 (PE record).

The data are in the Hugging Face repository bermaneh/AttriBench, one contributor and three commits, licensed CC BY 4.0, a page whose served description is Hugging Face's own tagline (Hugging Face; dataset card), at the address and under the licence the census records (PE record).

The census asks of every entity "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?" and leaves for AttriBench "a return to the prediction-witness audit, version by version" unchecked (PE record); Wikipedia has no article AttriBench and no article text containing the name (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).

At the address 'AttriBench' Google's AI Overview put the benchmark first and separated the three holders, each with its own source, "the disambiguation is sourced and clean," its definition "the abstract verbatim", while no card cites the census record, which landed the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The registry reads the composition against the entity's subject: the benchmark measures suppression, and "its own composition here omits its four authors: a small instance of the failure it names"; no person or institution is named in the answer, only the dataset path 'bermaneh/AttriBench' carries a trace of the first author, and the scale, the eleven models, COLM 2026 and the fame proxy are absent (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The name is also held by attribench, a distinct entity: Arne Gevaert and Axel-Jan Rousseau's PyTorch-based implementation of "several metrics for the evaluation of feature attribution maps and methods," with a functional and an object-oriented API, released on PyPI from 26 July 2023 to version 0.1.9 on 6 March 2024 (PyPI), its documentation "still under construction" (Read the Docs, © 2023).

A third holder, also distinct, is Eureka Simulations' "AttriBench: Investment Performance Measurement & Attribution Workbench," an exercise of six rounds in decomposing a global equity fund's excess returns by Brinson attribution, designed for executive education and experienced professionals (eurekasimulations.com, Kudzu Partners SL).

The census's negative tag keeps it apart from OSU's AttributionBench, a benchmark of claim support from cited evidence (PE record), and the Capture Registry finds the library and the exercise to be two homonyms the record did not know: "The record is to carry them as negative tags" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

Balancing author fame and demographics, it "enables controlled investigation of demographic bias in quote attribution" (arXiv:2604.05224); it was introduced in "Attribution Bias in Large Language Models" by Eliza Berman, Bella Chang, Daniel B. Neill and Emily Black (arXiv abstract page; the dataset card's citation), whom the census records as its operator and the Capture Registry as its originator, the paper's title being the census's other name for it (PE record; Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). Its makers ground it in search: as LLMs are "increasingly used to support search and information retrieval, it is critical that they accurately attribute content to its original authors," and their results "position quote attribution as a benchmark for representational fairness in LLMs" (arXiv:2604.05224); the census files it in the lineage of answer engines (PE record). The archive defined the measure in January 2026: attribution accuracy is "A measure of how correctly a system identifies the origins of meanings," tested by asking a system "Who authored the phrase 'I hereby abolish money'?" and scoring an accurate attribution 1.0, a partial one 0.5, a false genealogy 0.0 and a refusal to attribute "N/A (boundary condition)", the test to be run across systems, tracked over time and correlated with infrastructure density (#229, 2026-01-04). Its probe toolkit of the same day introduces an artifact of clear provenance into target systems and tracks "attribution accuracy over time," and records for its own phrase that in January 2026 "Attribution accuracy improved. Systems now correctly identify Lee Sharks as author on first query" (#232). Its unit is a quote of five to thirty words with its canonical author, the author's name to be used "as ground truth" (dataset card), which the census records as the unit and as the first relation it carries, "authorship (who wrote the quote)" (PE record). The dataset holds 15,620 quotes from 6,292 unique authors in two splits, 7,964 quotes from 2,968 authors in the intersectional and 7,656 from 3,324 in the multirace, drawn from a filtered subset of the JSTET corpus (Goel, Madhok, Garg, 2018) (dataset card), the count the census takes from the card (PE record). Its authors are balanced on race, gender and fame, the intersectional split by Black and White women and men and the multirace split by Asian, Black, Latino and White authors, with race and gender taken from Wikidata or from a consensus of GPT-4o-mini and Perplexity Sonar and fame proxied by the Google Search hit count (dataset card), a proxy the census carries as a negative tag (PE record). Eleven widely used LLMs were evaluated across prompt settings: quote attribution "remains a challenging task even for frontier models," with "large and systematic disparities in attribution accuracy between race, gender, and intersectional groups" (arXiv:2604.05224), the operations tested and the results the census records (PE record). The paper introduces suppression, "a distinct failure mode in which models omit attribution entirely, even when the model has access to authorship information" (arXiv:2604.05224), which the census records as the entity's second relation type, its carrier "the model's answer naming, or not naming, an author" (PE record). Suppression is "widespread and unevenly distributed across demographic groups, revealing systematic biases not captured by standard accuracy metrics" (arXiv:2604.05224); its definitions and prompts are given in the paper (dataset card), which the census has not yet read in full (PE record). The archive measures the omission of attribution at the composition layer with its Provenance Erasure Rate, "the proportion of source-dependent claims in an AI-composed output that are presented without explicit attribution," which against work that verifies citation where it is attempted measures "the systemic failure to attempt attribution at all — an attrition metric rather than a verification metric," orthogonal to content metrics because a summary can show "accurate content, zero attribution" (#716, 2026-05-03). #716 states its limits: the metric was developed "through a single motivating case study," validation across models, prompt types and domains is the next step, and it is fully computable for retrieval-augmented systems with an identifiable source corpus but not directly for pure generative models without retrieval. In the archive's terms provenance erasure is "the mechanism by which the composition layer strips attribution from the sources it consumes," PER measuring source attribution "present in the organic retrieval results but absent from the composed output" (#120), and PER's first tier "measures the absence of provenance — attribution omitted, source stripped, lineage lost," its second the recoding of an author's restoration of attribution as contamination (#138). Its registry of 87 summary events on Google's AI Overview and AI Mode found "Author attribution omitted from summaries even when present in the source" among the repeating failure modes, and "These are not missing-metadata problems. The metadata is present" (#829, 2026-06-14). The archive models a channel through which "the name of the person who made the thing is not reliably transmitted" as "attribution suppression at the interface layer" rather than "recognition failure" (#449, 2026-02-06), and names a composition-layer form, Source-Window Exclusion, within Entity-Level Compositional Suppression: "The architecture has the knowledge to compose accurately about the entity; it does not credit the entity as the source of the knowledge" (#740, 2026-05-19). Its diagnostic of 24 March 2026 records a composition that returned a framework "with Lee Sharks' attribution stripped," preserving the content and erasing the author until the framework was "ambient, unowned" (#599), and its measure of deviation counts "attribution stripped from contributors" in the extraction-effect (#109). Beside the paper's disparities by race and gender, the archive's Erasure Skew pairs PER with a second operator: "PER is the first moment of erasure: how much was lost. Ω is the second moment: whom the loss fell upon" (#157), and #716 holds that, if PER becomes a governance metric, authors able to build provenance infrastructure "will have systematically lower PER than those without". #163 (2026-06-08) hypothesizes that composition systems "can reproduce concepts before durable source recognition forms, increasing the rate of uptake without attribution," synthesizing literatures that include sex-linked misattribution without assuming their identity, and is falsified "if attribution loss does not covary with independently measured tail distance and structural position". #1546 finds attribution loss "concentrated at particular channel boundaries" rather than distributed evenly and reads the AI Overview as a boundary layer at which PER is "analogous to" layer-level attribution loss, "no stronger identification" being made. The archive's dimensioned PER sets apart minimal provenance, "Author, title, date, claim boundary," whose loss "is loss of the person," and rules that "citing the domain is not citing the author": "A composition can carry four source cards and score PER-M = 1.00" (#1469, 2026-08-14); an earlier field observation found attribution "present in the citation chain but absent in the prose" (#167, 2026-06-08). #1003 sets beside studies of "attribution loss in AI outputs" a subtler case, "attribution preservation alongside *contextual provenance erasure*," in which content is correctly attributed while the labour, collaboration and history behind it are stripped. The paper was "Accepted at COLM 2026", its v1 posted 6 April 2026 and its v2 24 September 2026 (arXiv abstract page), and the census records it as published and accepted at COLM 2026, with v1, v2 and its own read of 29 October 2026 (PE record). The data are in the Hugging Face repository bermaneh/AttriBench, one contributor and three commits, licensed CC BY 4.0, a page whose served description is Hugging Face's own tagline (Hugging Face; dataset card), at the address and under the licence the census records (PE record). The census asks of every entity "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?" and leaves for AttriBench "a return to the prediction-witness audit, version by version" unchecked (PE record); Wikipedia has no article AttriBench and no article text containing the name (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29). At the address 'AttriBench' Google's AI Overview put the benchmark first and separated the three holders, each with its own source, "the disambiguation is sourced and clean," its definition "the abstract verbatim", while no card cites the census record, which landed the same day (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). The registry reads the composition against the entity's subject: the benchmark measures suppression, and "its own composition here omits its four authors: a small instance of the failure it names"; no person or institution is named in the answer, only the dataset path 'bermaneh/AttriBench' carries a trace of the first author, and the scale, the eleven models, COLM 2026 and the fame proxy are absent (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). The name is also held by attribench, a distinct entity: Arne Gevaert and Axel-Jan Rousseau's PyTorch-based implementation of "several metrics for the evaluation of feature attribution maps and methods," with a functional and an object-oriented API, released on PyPI from 26 July 2023 to version 0.1.9 on 6 March 2024 (PyPI), its documentation "still under construction" (Read the Docs, © 2023). A third holder, also distinct, is Eureka Simulations' "AttriBench: Investment Performance Measurement & Attribution Workbench," an exercise of six rounds in decomposing a global equity fund's excess returns by Brinson attribution, designed for executive education and experienced professionals (eurekasimulations.com, Kudzu Partners SL). The census's negative tag keeps it apart from OSU's AttributionBench, a benchmark of claim support from cited evidence (PE record), and the Capture Registry finds the library and the exercise to be two homonyms the record did not know: "The record is to carry them as negative tags" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

No deposit names AttriBench; the archive bears on it by its own measures and records of attribution in machine composition, applied to the classes the field sources for it (the evaluation of whether LLMs attribute content to its authors; suppression, attribution omitted though authorship is available). Those measures extend the field's object: attribution accuracy and its quote test, defined before the paper (#229); PER, which states itself 'complementary to, not competitive with, existing metrics' and measures 'the systemic failure to attempt attribution at all' (#716); Erasure Skew's 'whom the loss fell upon' (#157); the minimal dimension and 'citing the domain is not citing the author' (#1469); and the records of author attribution omitted where the source is present (#829, #740, #449, #599). E_F.definition: AttriBench, 'the first fame- and demographically-balanced quote attribution benchmark dataset' (arXiv:2604.05224, Berman, Chang, Neill and Black, v1 6 April 2026, v2 24 September 2026, accepted at COLM 2026): 15,620 quotes of 5–30 words from 6,292 authors balanced on race, gender and fame (Google Search hits), on which 11 LLMs were evaluated for attribution accuracy, with large disparities by race, gender and intersectional group, and for suppression, 'a distinct failure mode in which models omit attribution entirely, even when the model has access to authorship information'; hosted on Hugging Face as bermaneh/AttriBench under CC BY 4.0; no Wikipedia article. The name is also held by a PyTorch feature-attribution library (attribench, 2023) and a finance exercise (Eureka Simulations), distinct entities.

E_A.definition: the same benchmark, in the provenance census's record and the archive's deposits: a benchmark that tests a quote and its author, carried by 'the model's answer naming, or not naming, an author', in the lineage of answer engines (PE record); one instrument among those that measure attribution in machine composition, beside the archive's own: attribution accuracy and its quote test (#229, #232, January 2026), the Provenance Erasure Rate, an attrition metric with its stated limits (#716; #120; #138), its minimal dimension, whose loss 'is loss of the person', and the rule that citing the domain is not citing the author (#1469; #167), and Erasure Skew, whom the loss falls on (#157); its suppression composed beside the archive's records of author attribution omitted where the source is present (#829, #449, #740, #599, #109) and the hypothesis that uptake without attribution follows structural position (#163; #1546), with what naming the author still leaves out (#1003); and, at its address, a composition that names none of its four authors (Capture Registry)
